tldr: To adapt pretrained VLA (vision-language-action) models online to fine-grained lab tasks on real robots, this study trains visual anchors with training-time-only region annotations while boosting learner update speed by roughly 10x using KV cache reuse and single-step action generation.
hero_caption: Overview and motivation of GRAFT. (a) Conventional VLAs struggle with gaze alignment on tiny contact areas and suffer heavy computational overhead. (b) GRAFT introduces local visual grounding via visual anchors and KV cache reuse. (c) This substantially improves success rates across four biomedical manipulation tasks while speeding up learner updates by 9.94x.
overview:
Large-scale pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models exhibit strong generalization, but directly adapting them to biomedical manipulation tasks—such as pipette tip attachment or centrifuge tube loading, where millimeter-level contact precision is essential—remains challenging. Fine-tuning via online reinforcement learning (RL) on a real robot with sparse, task-level scalar rewards (success or failure) requires massive trial-and-error just to discover where to look in an image. On top of that, the heavy computational cost of VLM inference and replay-based updates creates a critical bottleneck, preventing the policy from completing enough updates within a limited wall-clock adaptation budget.

To solve this, the authors introduce GRAFT (Grounded Reinforcement Adaptation for Fast Task Learning), an online adaptation framework that balances local visual grounding with computational efficiency. It hinges on two core ideas. First, it uses offline candidate region proposals purely during training to provide auxiliary supervision for view-specific visual anchors, completely removing the proposal generator at real-robot test time for lightweight inference. Instead of collapsing multiple proposals into a single combined mask, GRAFT supervises them with an identity-free loss (FreeDice) that avoids rigid anchor-to-region assignments. Second, it caches and reuses the frozen VLM's key-value (KV) states during replay updates and swaps iterative diffusion action generation for a single-step Consistency Policy, slashing computation inside the learning loop.

Using a real-robot JAKA arm, the authors evaluated GRAFT across four fine-grained biomedical manipulation tasks, allocating a strict 45-minute online adaptation budget per method. GRAFT raised the final success rate by 25 percentage points (reaching 82.5% overall) compared to an approach that simply merges region proposals, and achieved a 32.5 percentage point boost over the RL-CP baseline. Learner update throughput also increased by up to 9.94x, clearly demonstrating how policies can quickly pinpoint local contact cues and adapt within limited physical robot time.
contributions: Proposed a grounding mechanism that learns view-specific visual anchors via identity-free multi-region supervision used only during training, eliminating any need for masks or region detectors at deployment
Combined frozen VLM prefix KV caching with single-step action generation to accelerate online learner update speed by up to nearly 10x
Demonstrated substantial improvements in success rates and reductions in human interventions across four real-robot biomedical manipulation tasks under strictly matched 45-minute adaptation budgets

sections.heading: Where GRAFT fits: Fine-grained bio-manipulation and faster VLAs
sections.summary: This section organizes the context across three areas: laboratory automation, visual grounding, and computationally efficient real-robot RL. Rather than proposing a new RL algorithm, this work targets representation learning so pretrained policies can efficiently learn where to look under limited physical runtime.
sections.details:
This section outlines three research domains anchoring GRAFT and clarifies where the method stands.

- Robot learning for lab automation: Automating chemistry and biology tasks has gained notable traction, but it presents unique hurdles absent in standard tabletop manipulation, such as tiny contact surfaces, transparent or reflective containers, and strict procedural protocols. Most prior studies have focused on building simulators, workflow reasoning, or reward design; this work tackles the complementary problem of how a pretrained model can acquire task-relevant visual cues from limited real-robot interactions.

- Grounding and multi-view perception in VLA manipulation: To improve spatial awareness in VLAs, earlier works introduced 3D representations, runtime crop inputs, or auxiliary training tasks like gaze and contact prediction. GRAFT falls under the auxiliary training signal umbrella, but it is novel in processing multiple camera views separately and supervising region proposals independently rather than fusing them into a single mask. It also requires zero heavy object detectors at test time.

- Real-robot RL and VLA efficiency: Off-policy RL using demonstrations and human-in-the-loop intervention strategies has delivered strong empirical results. However, adapting within a tight wall-clock time limit demands faster inference and gradient updates. While prior efforts accelerated the actor via action chunking or parallel decoding, GRAFT targets the learner side by eliminating redundant forward passes on frozen prefixes during replay updates, dramatically raising update throughput.

sections.heading: How GRAFT works: Training-only region guidance and cached ultra-fast learning
sections.summary: GRAFT adopts an asynchronous actor-learner architecture featuring view-specific anchors, training-time-only identity-free multi-region supervision (FreeDice), frozen prefix KV caching, and a single-step Consistency Policy. Deployment requires no extra detectors, ensuring lightweight yet precise execution.
sections.details:
GRAFT's architecture and training pipeline are carefully engineered to maximize rapid online adaptation on real hardware.

### Problem setup and deployment boundaries (III-A)
At timestep $t$, the robot observes side-view and wrist-view RGB images, a language instruction $l$, and proprioceptive robot state $q_t$. It outputs an action chunk of $H=10$ steps (position, orientation, and gripper state). A frozen VLM prefix encodes these inputs into visual tokens $X_t^v$, context $c_t$, and KV states. Crucially, offline-generated region masks $\mathcal{M}_t^v$ are used exclusively for computing loss terms during training; at deployment, neither masks nor detectors are ever fed into the robot.

### Efficient replay adaptation (III-B)
On the learner side, the system caches and reuses the frozen VLM prefix KV states and visual tokens pulled from replay buffer transitions. This skips the heavy VLM forward pass, allowing updates to focus solely on the trainable visual anchors and action heads. Furthermore, instead of multi-step denoising via Flow Matching, GRAFT uses a Consistency Policy that samples actions in a single forward pass, substantially trimming action generation overhead.

### View-specific visual anchors (III-C)
The model allocates $N_v=8$ anchor templates separately for the side view and the wrist view. Through cross-attention with their respective view tokens, each anchor extracts observation-dependent anchor features $z_i^v$. These are gated and reweighted using the global context before being passed to the action expert.

### Training-only multi-region guidance (III-D)
This is the core highlight of the approach. When multiple candidate regions exist, collapsing them into one combined mask discards distinct, critical sub-part information. To avoid this, GRAFT introduces the FreeDice loss. Using a soft-minimum ($\operatorname{smin}$), it bids bi-directionally to match each proposal to the closest anchor while ensuring every anchor attends to some valid proposal. Because it enforces no fixed identity mapping between anchors and regions, the anchors autonomously learn to capture complementary and diverse local features.

### Online adaptation and inference (III-E)
Online adaptation runs asynchronously. The actor executes actions and logs transitions—including human interventions—into the replay buffer. The learner samples evenly from offline demonstrations and online replay data, updating the policy via Twin Critic Q-learning (action-value maximization), Behavior Cloning loss, and periodically applied visual grounding loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ground}}$.

sections.heading: 45-minute real-robot adaptation demonstrates clear success gains and speedups
sections.summary: Across four challenging biomedical manipulation tasks with matched 45-minute adaptation budgets, GRAFT outperformed GRAFT-Union (which merges regions) by 25 percentage points and the RL-CP baseline by 32.5 percentage points, while boosting learner update throughput by roughly 10x.
sections.details:
Experiments were structured around four key questions: Does multi-region supervision help? Can it adapt within a tight time budget? How much does computation improve? Does it achieve detector-free grounding at deployment?

### Real-robot tasks and protocol (IV-A)
Using a JAKA robotic arm, four tasks were evaluated: (1) Petri Dish De-lidding, (2) Centrifuge Tube Loading, (3) Precision Liquid Transfer, and (4) Pipette Tip Attachment. Target objects were perturbed randomly by $\pm 30\,\mathrm{mm}$. All methods received the same 10 demonstrations, and online adaptation was fixed to exactly 45 minutes of wall-clock time.

### Baselines (IV-B)
- RL-FM: RL paired with a standard Flow Matching action generator.
- RL-CP: Replaces action generation with a single-step Consistency Policy.
- GRAFT-Union: An ablation that introduces visual anchors but supervises them with a single union mask.
- GRAFT: The proposed method (individual multi-region guidance using the identity-free FreeDice loss).

### Task success rates and learning curves (IV-C)
In the final 10 evaluation episodes, GRAFT achieved 33 successes out of 40 trials (82.5%), marking a 25 percentage point lead over GRAFT-Union's 23/40 (57.5%). On the centrifuge tube task in particular, which demands tracking the tube, gripper, and loading slot at once, GRAFT jumped to 9/10 compared to GRAFT-Union's 2/10. Furthermore, human intervention rates dropped near zero toward the end of training, showing the policy learned high-precision retries and contact maneuvers autonomously.

### Learner update efficiency (IV-D)
Measuring offline update throughput, RL-FM without KV caching managed 1.99 steps/s and RL-CP reached 2.21 steps/s. Enabling prefix KV caching accelerated RL-CP to 21.96 steps/s—a 9.94x speedup. Coupling single-step generation with prefix caching allowed far more gradient updates within the wall-clock limit.

### Grounding visualizations (IV-E)
Inspecting attention maps revealed that while GRAFT-Union spread its attention broadly and diffusely around targets, GRAFT focused sharply on contact-critical local zones, such as the pipette tip and tube rims. The model also naturally split roles across camera angles: global alignment in the side view and fine insertion details in the wrist view.

sections.heading: Summary and what comes next
sections.summary: GRAFT makes online VLA adaptation practical by combining training-only region-guided visual anchors with KV caching and single-step action generation. Since the current policy acts reactively, integrating temporal context for longer-horizon tasks remains an open direction.
sections.details:
This paper presented GRAFT, a new framework for online adaptation of pretrained VLAs to fine-grained biomedical manipulation. By supervising view-specific visual anchors with training-time-only proposals, the policy preserves lightweight inference without detectors while reliably focusing on task-critical local cues.

In addition, caching prefix KV states and adopting a single-step Consistency action model sped up learner update throughput by up to nearly 10x. This enabled GRAFT to decisively outperform baseline methods within an extremely tight 45-minute real-robot training window.

As a limitation noted by the authors, the current policy operates reactively from single frames, lacking an explicit representation of past action history or task progress. Incorporating temporal context will be essential for long-horizon workflows where task-relevant gaze targets shift across consecutive stages.

takeaways: Teaching with masks strictly during training while removing them at test time enables both fast inference and sharp visual grounding
When providing multi-region guidance, preserving individual region diversity through an identity-free loss (FreeDice) is far more effective than collapsing them into a single union mask
For real-robot online VLA learning, combining frozen prefix KV caching with single-step action generation (Consistency Policy) eliminates key update bottlenecks
In wall-clock-constrained robot adaptation, computational throughput per unit time matters just as much as sample efficiency
limitations: The policy is reactive (relying only on the current observation) and lacks memory to track long-horizon action history or overall task progress
Generating region proposals upfront requires offline segmentation models (such as SAM 2 or Grounding DINO) during data preparation
While validated across four tasks, generalization to more dynamic contact variations and wider assortments of tools remains to be tested
